content: Smoking is an activity in which a substance, most commonly tobacco, is burned, and the resulting smoke is inhaled or tasted. This practice is primarily recreational, as the combustion process releases active substances like nicotine, which are absorbed through the lungs. Smoking can also be part of religious rituals, used to induce trances or achieve spiritual enlightenment. The most common method of smoking today is through cigarettes, which may be either industrially manufactured or hand-rolled using loose tobacco and rolling paper. Other less common methods include pipes, cigars, bongs, and hookahs. Smoking remains one of the most prevalent forms of recreational drug use. The history of smoking dates back to as early as 5000 BC. Tobacco cultivation began in the Americas around 3000 BC. A significant turning point in the history of smoking occurred during the era of global exploration, when sailors introduced tobacco to different parts of the world. Smoking can be categorized based on the number of cigarettes consumed daily, with classifications such as heavy and non-heavy smoking. It can also be classified by duration, distinguishing between acute and chronic smokers. Nicotine, the primary active substance in cigarettes, is rapidly absorbed through the lungs and quickly diffuses into the brain. There, it binds to nicotinic acetylcholine receptors, stimulating the release of dopamine and other neurotransmitters. This process is responsible for the pleasurable sensations associated with smoking. The causes of smoking are multifactorial and are closely linked to its risk factors. Tobacco use is the leading cause of preventable disease, disability, and death in the United States. It accounts for over 480,000 deaths annually, which is equivalent to one in every five deaths. In 2015, approximately 15.1% of U.S. adults aged 18 years or older were current cigarette smokers, representing an estimated 36.5 million adults. Smoking is more prevalent among men than women and is most common in adults aged 25 to 44 years. It is also more frequently observed among non-Hispanic American Indians/Alaska Natives compared to other racial groups. Common risk factors for smoking include poor family relationships, unemployment, alcohol addiction, use of illicit drugs, anxiety disorders, and genetic predisposition. Screening for smoking is conducted during every visit to a physician. This involves asking detailed questions about the patient’s smoking status and history. The U.S. Preventive Services Task Force recommends that clinicians inquire about tobacco use in all patients and provide interventions to help those who use tobacco quit. Smoking may initially be asymptomatic and relatively easy to quit. However, if left unaddressed, it can lead to a wide range of symptoms affecting multiple organ systems. Smoking is a major cause of carcinomas and can ultimately result in death. Its complications are not confined to a single organ system, with the cardiovascular and respiratory systems being the most commonly affected. Smoking increases the risk of coronary artery disease by two to four times and is a leading cause of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD). Most cases of lung cancer are attributed to cigarette smoking. Smoking is the leading preventable cause of death in the United States. Smoking cessation has been shown to improve prognosis in patients with lung cancer. The diagnosis of tobacco use is primarily based on a confidential interview or history-taking. Symptoms of chronic smoking include fatigue, shortness of breath during exertion, snoring, sleep apnea, retrosternal discomfort, heartburn, weight loss, breathlessness, sputum production, chest pain, leg pain, loss of appetite, and bloody sputum. Physical examination findings in smokers may include tachycardia, hypertension, rapid breathing, clothing with a smoke odor, stained teeth or fingernails, a hoarse voice, and wheezing. There are no specific diagnostic laboratory findings associated with smoking. Chest X-rays do not show findings directly attributable to smoking but can be used to diagnose complications such as carcinomas, pulmonary fibrosis, and COPD. Similarly, ultrasound imaging does not reveal findings specific to smoking but can help identify complications like carcinomas. CT scans do not show findings directly related to smoking but are useful in confirming complications such as carcinomas, pulmonary fibrosis, COPD, and stroke. MRI findings are not specific to smoking but can also confirm complications like carcinomas, pulmonary fibrosis, COPD, and stroke. No additional imaging studies are specific to smoking. Breath carbon monoxide testing can be used to detect recent smoking within the past 24 hours. Smoking cessation can be supported through various strategies. The 5 As approach—Ask, Assess, Advise, Assist, and Arrange follow-up—is a general framework. Non-pharmacological methods include nicotine gum and nicotine patches, while pharmacological options include bupropion, varenicline, inhalers, and nasal sprays. Surgical intervention is not recommended for smoking itself but may be necessary to manage complications such as carcinomas, stroke, coronary artery disease, and ectopic pregnancy. Secondary prevention strategies for smoking are similar to those used in primary prevention.
